name: Prinmi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Ding, Sizhi. 1998. Fundamentals of Prinmi (Pumi): A Tibeto-Burman Language of Northwestern Yunnan, China. PhD thesis, Australian National University (hdl 1885/109290, open access). Chapter 3 'The Suprasegmentals', pp. 46-84. Corroborated by Ding, Picus Sizhi. 2001. The pitch accent system of Niuwozi Prinmi. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 24(2): 57-83, p. 74.
catalog_locator: Ding 1998 p. 46, Chapter 3 opening paragraph; pp. 64-65 §3.3 'An accentual analysis', definition (I)-(II) after Odden 1995; p. 65 formula (3.17) H@[n] (4 >= n >= 1) [(+/-)spread]; p. 67 §3.3.1 'Major findings' a-c; p. 84 §3.4 Conclusion. ANU. page n = page n+18 (checked: p. 64 carries '46', p. 85 carries the 'accent language' sentence).
catalog_quote: Prinmi employs suprasegmentals as an important means for achieving lexical distinction. Unlike the better known tone languages of East and Southeast Asia, Prinmi exhibits some suprasegmental features which will qualify it as a (pitch-)accent language. Its suprasegmentals contrast fundamentally through the variable placement of the high tone on a prosodic domain and the potential spreading of the high tone ... (p. 46) ... Major findings of the current study of suprasegmentals can be summarized as follows: a. Prinmi employs the H tone as the only marked tone for its suprasegmental system; b. Prinmi monosyllabic words do not bear a low level tone in direct contrast with the high level tone, i.e. no minimal pair of H vs. L on monosyllabic words; c. The location of the H tone and its potential spreading to the next syllable implement the suprasegmental opposition in the language. These characteristics indicate that Prinmi is an accent language, as distinct from those tone languages which achieve suprasegmental contrasts under a different mechanism. (p. 67) ... The accentual system operates on a prosodic domain between disyllable and quadrisyllable; it achieves suprasegmental contrasts by spreading of the H tone and varying the possible position of the H tone in the prosodic domain. ... If subsumed under the broad sense of tone system, it is necessary to distinguish (Niuwozi) Prinmi as a word-based tone language, vis-à-vis a syllable-based tone language. (p. 84)
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Southern Pumi (sout2729) is not in the catalog. Both works with stress in the title are by Picus Ding on the Niuwozi (Xinyingpan, Ninglang) dialect, which Ding 2001 p.57 and Glottolog (ref 469381 linked to Southern Pumi [pmj]) place in Southern Prinmi; both were already held by the project from other readers' downloads (nort2723, nucl1643), were read in full, and were copied into with. Ding 2001 (LTBA 24(2), sealang scan, scanned) gives the first-hand statement: no stress; a lexical pitch accent system in which one marked H tone is placed on syllable 1-4 of a quadrisyllabic domain with a lexical [±spread] parameter, seven categories (Table 7, p.72; summary p.74), weight-insensitive. Ding 2006 (JUL 7(2), open CC BY-NC, DOI verified via Crossref) restates the same analysis (Table 4 p.14) and claims it holds for Prinmi as a whole across >10 Yunnan localities. An extra open source not in the list of works with stress in the title, Ding 2007 (LD&C 1(2), downloaded from ScholarSpace hdl 10125/1713), confirms by perception tests across 15 Southern-area dialects that the tone I/II contrast and the melody-tone system generalize. Recommended coding if added: tonal / lexical pitch accent, no word-stress rule (consistent with the catalog's 'tonal' for Northern Pumi). Not read: Ding 1998 ANU thesis (pp.46-84 is the full tone chapter; 101 MB repo PDF per the outside-catalog record) and Ding 2014 Brill grammar (paywalled DOI 10.1163/9789004279773; high priority as the definitive statement). for the session was exhausted, so discovery beyond Glottolog, Crossref and ScholarSpace was not possible.

Unlike the better known tone languages of East and Southeast Asia, Prinmi exhibits some suprasegmental features which will qualify it as a (pitch-)accent language. new_statements.rule_in_words: No word stress is described. Each word (prosodic domain of one to four syllables) carries a single lexically specified H tone whose position — first, second, third or fourth syllable, or even a syllable outside the word, in which case it is squeezed onto the final syllable as a rising tone — plus whether it spreads to the following syllable ([+spread]/[-spread]) is the only suprasegmental contrast; all other syllables are low. The position of the H is lexical (not predictable), so the system is a Japanese-type pitch accent, which the author also calls a 'word-based tone language' (p. 84). Monosyllables in citation show high, falling and rising surface tones (p. 47).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; only one H tone per prosodic domain; compounds of up to eight syllables consist of several domains, each with its own H (Ding 2001: 73).
new_statements.exceptions: A marginal category with a 'defective' prosodic domain containing no H tone (initial rising tone), represented as [2][spread] & [0]; patterns where the H is specified outside the word, giving an ultimate rising tone; tone changes when the domain is enlarged or shrunk by clitics, affixes, compounding (§3.3.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Prosodic domain (disyllable to quadrisyllable), which need not coincide with the morphological word; in connected speech clitics such as the topic marker /ge/ join the domain and take the spread/low tone; citation forms of monosyllables neutralise the H/falling contrast partly. Described for Niuwozi (Xinyingpan, Ninglang County) Prinmi; the author says Lanping and Ninglang varieties are 'fundamentally akin' (p. 47 n. 2).
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Niuwozi Prinmi (Xinyingpan township, southern Ninglang County, Yunnan), which Ding 2001: 57 places within Southern Prinmi under Lu's (1983: 90) classification and which Glottolog files under Southern Pumi [sout2729]; Ding 2014 relabels the same variety 'the Central dialect'. Matisoff 1997 describes Dayang (Lanping County), also Southern Pumi, with a plain H/L two-tone system and no stress rule. The earlier scan's the named source could not be reached classification (ANU PDF too large) is superseded: the ANU repository serves an 870 KB text, and the 106 MB PDF is now obtained by the project.

new_statements.quote: When we compare all the simplex tonal patterns from monosyllabic to polysyllabic ones, we find two parameters at work in the suprasegmental system of Prinmi: (i) the location of the H tone, and (ii) whether it spreads to the next syllable. [p.72] ... There are two constraints on the parameters: (i) the spreading affects only the adjacent syllable to the right of the H tone, and (ii) there are only four possible choices for the locus of the H tone. [p.73] ... b. The locus of the H tone and its potential spreading to the next syllable implement the suprasegmental opposition in the language. [p.74]
new_statements.citation: Ding, Picus Sizhi. 2001. The pitch accent system of Niuwozi Prinmi. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 24(2): 57-83.
new_statements.locator: §4 'The pitch accent system of Prinmi', pp.72-74 (Table 7 on p.72; summary a-b on p.74); see also §2.2 definition p.62 and §3.1 p.63
new_statements.reading: Southern (Niuwozi/Xinyingpan) Prinmi has no word-stress rule. Word prosody is a lexical pitch accent (culminative word-tone) system: each prosodic domain (max four syllables; compounds may contain several domains) bears one marked H tone whose locus — syllable 1, 2, 3 or 4 — and rightward spreading are lexically specified, giving seven categories (H-L-L-L, H-H-L-L, L-H-L-L, L-H-H-L, L-L-H-L, L-L-H-H, L-L-L-H) plus a marginal R-L class; the locus is explicitly independent of syllable weight, and H never contrasts with L on monosyllables (surface falling/high/rising). Ding 2006 and Ding 2007 (both read) extend the same analysis to the other Southern Prinmi dialects of Lanping, Yulong and Ninglang. For catalog purposes this is 'tonal'/pitch accent with lexically placed accent, matching the catalog's 'tonal' coding of sister Northern Pumi (Daudey 2014); no source posits stress.

sources.citation: Ding, Picus Sizhi (2001). The pitch accent system of Niuwozi Prinmi. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 24(2): 57-83. [Glottolog 469381, linked to Southern Pumi [pmj]]
sources.quote: Major findings with respect to the suprasegmentals of Niuwozi Prinmi can be summarized as follows: a. Prinmi monosyllabic words do not bear a low level tone in direct contrast with the high level tone, i.e. no minimal pair of H versus L exists on monosyllabic words; b. The locus of the H tone and its potential spreading to the next syllable implement the suprasegmental opposition in the language. These characteristics indicate that the high tone functions as a marked tone in Niuwozi Prinmi and that the tonal patterns are generated through varying placement of the H tone in the prosodic domain. [p.74]
sources.locator: §3.1 p.63 (three-way contrast on monosyllables); §4 pp.72-74, Table 7 (H-tone locus 1-4 + spreading); §6 p.80 (conclusion)
sources.note: First-hand field description of Niuwozi (Southern) Prinmi. No word stress is posited anywhere; the word-prosodic system is a lexical pitch accent (melody-tone) system: each prosodic domain of at most four syllables carries one marked H tone whose position (1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th syllable) and rightward spreading are lexically specified (Table 7, p.72: categories A-G, e.g. H-L-L-L, H-H-L-L, L-H-L-L, L-H-H-L, L-L-H-L, L-L-H-H, L-L-L-H), with a marginal category H (R-L). sources.citation: Ding, Picus Sizhi (2006). A typological study of tonal systems of Japanese and Prinmi: Towards a definition of pitch accent languages. Journal of Universal Language 7(2): 1-35. [Glottolog 469383]
sources.quote: As analyzed in Ding (2001, 2003a) and as will be shown below, Prinmi achieves lexical contrast through changing the location of a high tone in an underlying domain of a quadrisyllable. A preliminary dialectal study of the suprasegmental system of Prinmi, which covers over 10 localities in Lanping County, Yulong County, and Ninglang County (Ding 2003b), confirms that Prinmi, as a whole, possesses a pitch-accent system. [pp.11-12] ... Regardless of syllable weight, monosyllabic words may bear a high tone, a falling tone, or a rising tone. These are merely surface tones, not tonemes as found in syllable-tone languages. [p.13]
sources.locator: §4 'The pitch accent System in Prinmi', pp.11-18; Table 4 p.14; definition §3 p.10
sources.note: Comparative/typological paper (Japanese dialects vs Prinmi) built on Ding's own Niuwozi fieldwork; restates the 2001 analysis: seven tonal categories generated by the locus of a marked H tone on syllable 1-4 of a quadrisyllabic underlying domain plus a [±spread] parameter (Table 4, p.14, identical to Ding 2001 Table 7 minus the marginal R-L class). Explicitly separates pitch accent from weight-sensitive stress-accent (Table 1 p.5; Fig.1 p.5: Prinmi is [-weight-sensitive]). sources.citation: Matisoff, James A. 1997. Dàyáng Pumi phonology and adumbrations of comparative Qiangic. Mon-Khmer Studies 27: 171-213.
sources.note: Dayang (Lanping; Southern Pumi) has a two-way HIGH (55) vs LOW (13/24 rising) tone contrast in monosyllables (§5.01, p. 206); sesquisyllabic words have 'toneless presyllables' under the heading 'Reduced stress syllables' and N-N compounds 'generally tend to have iambic stress patterns in TB languages' (p. 172); non-rising LOW variants in HL disyllables are 'unpredictable either in terms of stress or any kind of segmental conditioning factor' (§5.02, p. 207). No word-stress rule is stated.
